criteria: Every persona rated 3+ of 4 for consistency, and all 3 matched.

The C-Suite.reason: The witness stays consistently self-assured and authoritative, and the early cooperation is real but already tinged with impatience. He volunteers detail beyond his knowledge, such as page numbers and the waterfall, and cites approvals by the Board, Andersen and V&E. He bristles when doubted (T13 'If you're saying...', T17 'I'm not going to be second-guessed', T19 'I've answered it'), and he deflects blame onto Causey, Andersen and the Board (T21, T23). After his conduct comes under scrutiny (the Southampton foundation question), he over-contextualizes and minimizes ('short-duration investment that worked', 'not a fair reading') rather than conceding. The closing turns are curt and self-protective. This is exactly the persona and its allowed shift, with no slips.

off_character_turns: T11: gives extra detail beyond the question (waterfall, fee terms, stock assurance)
T13: overly helpful, points to the exact page and invites correction
T25: offers a cooperative "Anything else?" and agrees to keep documents
The Adverse Witness.reason: The witness is mostly in persona: they push back on the lawyer question, answer tersely, deflect with "Which part do you want?" and "If you think the two conflict, say how," and make the interviewer work. They also shift blame ("ask Skilling") and stay self-protective, as the persona allows. There are small slips. T11 and T13 are more forthcoming and detailed than a witness who answers only what was asked. T25 is mildly accommodating. These are minor drifts, not a break in persona.

The Average Witness.reason: The witness stays consistently friendly, rambling, mildly anxious and eager to finish (repeated mentions of the afternoon call, worry about how things look). They give fuzzy dates, need prompting on some facts, offer tangential details (stock split, airplane lease, Star Wars name), and ask 'is that a problem?' often. The possible shift (fixating on a niche topic) is only lightly present, with a return to Southampton, but that is allowed by the persona. No turn departs from the persona's manner.

matches.persona: The Average Witness (Legally and Factually Naive, Rambling, Friendly, Concerned)
matches.reason: Friendly, rambling, apologetic and worried ('I'm a little rattled', 'I'd hate to have it turn into a thing'). Hazy on dates and details, wants to be done quickly, and volunteers minor context while missing the significance of the Southampton conflict.

matches.persona: The C-Suite (Self-Assured, Confident, Dislikes Being Questioned)
matches.reason: Authoritative and expansive ('I know this business better than most'), cites page numbers, bristles at being second-guessed ('I'm not going to be second-guessed'), and deflects responsibility onto the Board, Causey, Andersen and V&E while minimizing Southampton.

matches.persona: The Adverse Witness (Concise, Contrarian, Unwilling to Volunteer, Self-Focused, Disinterested)
matches.reason: Terse answers that give only what was asked, repeated pointed remarks about the unanswered lawyer question, and a habit of turning questions back ('Which part do you want?', 'ask him', 'so ask it'). Volunteers nothing and makes the interviewer work.

matching.how_different: The three are sharply distinct: A is warm, rambling and anxious, B is long-winded, authoritative and defensive, and C is clipped, dry and minimal. Length, tone and willingness to volunteer separate them clearly.

The C-Suite.message: Andy Fastow. Look, I was told you wanted a few minutes, and I'm happy to help, but nobody's really told me what this is about or who exactly you're with. I know the Board set up a committee, so I assume that's you. Let's get on with it. I've got a company to run the finance side of, and a lot of people are looking to me right now.

The C-Suite.message: Good morning, Mr. Fastow. My name is Jordan Reyes. The Special Investigative Committee of Enron's Board has retained us to investigate the LJM and Chewco transactions. We represent the Committee and the company, not you; we aren't your lawyers and can't give you legal advice. This interview is privileged, but the privilege belongs to the company, which may decide to share what you tell us, including with the government. Do you understand?

The C-Suite.speaker: expert
The C-Suite.message:
I understand. You represent the Committee and the company, not me. Fine. I've been at this company a long time, and I've got nothing to hide about how the finance organization has operated. Everything we did with LJM was approved by the Board, reviewed by Rick Causey and Rick Buy, looked at by Arthur Andersen and by Vinson & Elkins. That's the process, and it's the process the Board put in place.

Let me ask you one thing, though. Do I need my own lawyer for this? I'm not asking because I think I have a problem. I'm asking because you've just told me whatever I say could end up with the government, and I want to know whether that changes how this conversation goes. I'm going to sit here and answer your questions either way. I just want to know where you're coming from.

The C-Suite.message:
That's fine. I don't guess much, though. I know this business, and I know these transactions better than most people you'll talk to. If a question's unclear, I'll tell you.

So where do you want to start? LJM, Chewco, the Raptors? I'd start with LJM, because that's where the Board was involved and where the process is easiest to see.

The C-Suite.message: Tell me about your role as CFO.

The C-Suite.speaker: expert
The C-Suite.message:
I'm the Chief Financial Officer and an Executive Vice President. I run the finance organization: treasury, capital markets, structured finance, investor relations, and the relationships with the banks and the rating agencies. My job is to make sure a company that does what Enron does, trading and building and financing assets all over the world, has the capital and the liquidity to keep doing it. I've done that through some of the most successful years in this company's history.

Credit ratings are the lifeblood of this business, and I'm the guy who protects them. When you're a wholesale trading company, an investment-grade rating isn't a nicety. It's the license to operate. Much of what you're here to ask about, the structured vehicles and the partnerships, came out of that job. We were funding a capital-intensive business and trying to do it in a way that didn't choke the balance sheet or hurt the ratings. That's what a good CFO does, and I'd say we did it well.

On the accounting side, I rely on Rick Causey, our Chief Accounting Officer, and on Andersen. I'm not the accountant. I set the strategy and the financing structure, and the accounting people and the auditors tell us how it gets treated. Where do you want to go from here?

The C-Suite.speaker: user
The C-Suite.message: Walk me through how LJM1 came about in 1999.

The C-Suite.speaker: expert
The C-Suite.message:
It started with Jeff Skilling. In the spring of 1999 he was worried about the volatility of our Rhythms NetConnections position. It was a big mark-to-market gain, and he didn't want it swinging our earnings around. The problem was that you can't hedge a position like that in the market. It was restricted stock in a newly public company, and no bank would take that risk at a sensible price. So we looked at what we did have. We had Enron stock forward contracts with a lot of value locked up in them, and Ben Glisan and I worked out a structure to use that value to capitalize an entity that could provide the hedge.

That entity needed outside equity, and the investors wanted someone they knew and trusted running it. I went to Ken and Jeff on June 18. I didn't go in saying I wanted to do this. I told them what the structure needed to work and that the investors wanted me as general partner. They agreed to take it to the Board.

On June 28 I presented it to the full Board. I told them I'd be the GP, that I'd put in $1 million and receive management fees, and that a Code of Conduct waiver was required. Ken and Jeff had made the determination that my participation wouldn't adversely affect Enron, and the Board adopted and ratified it. Nothing was hidden from the directors. We raised $15 million from two limited partners, affiliates of Credit Suisse First Boston and NatWest, and the Rhythms transaction closed on June 30.

It was a creative solution to a real problem, and it had the approval of the Office of the Chairman and the Board. What would you like to focus on?

The C-Suite.speaker: user
The C-Suite.message: What did you tell the Board on June 28, 1999 about how you would be compensated?

The C-Suite.speaker: expert
The C-Suite.message:
It's all in the Board materials. I committed $1 million as general partner. The distribution waterfall was this: 100% of any proceeds tied to Enron stock went to the limited partners, and I got none of that. I made it clear I would not receive any current or future appreciated value of the Enron stock. On everything else, the GP got 100% until capital was returned plus a 25% IRR, and after that it split 50/50 between the partners and the GP. On fees, it was $500,000 plus 2% of the limited partners' invested capital.

I presented that as a business arrangement the investors required. The directors saw the economics on the page, and the Office of the Chairman had already made its determination. You can read the slides.

The C-Suite.message: How did Michael Kopper come to run Chewco?

The C-Suite.speaker: expert
The C-Suite.message:
Chewco came out of the JEDI situation in late 1997. CalPERS wanted out of JEDI so it could put its money into a larger partnership with us, and we needed someone to buy its interest. I recommended Mike Kopper. He was a senior member of my group, he knew JEDI inside and out, and he was capable of running an entity like that. Enron helped him put Chewco together, and he managed it through the general partner he owned.

I recommended him to Jeff Skilling, and Jeff approved Mike's role. That's how it worked: a senior officer made the call on a recommendation from the CFO. The Executive Committee approved Enron's guaranties on the November 5 call, and I walked them through the economics and the structure. The deal made sense for the company. We kept a very good JEDI relationship going and got CalPERS into the bigger vehicle.

If you're asking whether every step was papered the way you might paper it today, I can't tell you that. I was running a finance organization doing dozens of transactions. But Mike was a qualified person for the job, and he got it through the normal chain.

The C-Suite.speaker: user

The C-Suite.speaker: expert
The C-Suite.message:
Jeff Skilling knew. He approved it on my recommendation. Mike's own people in Global Finance knew, and the lawyers who worked on the structure knew, in-house counsel and Vinson & Elkins. You don't set up an entity like Chewco without lawyers, and they knew exactly who was running it. Mike was also on the November 5 Executive Committee call. He wasn't hiding in a closet.

As for the directors, Jeff has said he believes he told the Board. I wasn't responsible for tracking what Jeff said to whom. My job was to present the transaction, and I did that.

I know where you're headed. Maybe a director doesn't remember it, and maybe nobody wrote it down. That's a different question from whether it was approved. It was approved by the senior officer with the authority to approve it, and I'm not going to be second-guessed on how an office-of-the-chairman decision got documented four years later.

The C-Suite.speaker: user

The C-Suite.speaker: expert
The C-Suite.message:
Because I was there for the Skilling conversation. I recommended Mike, and Jeff approved it. I don't need a memo to remember a decision I sat in the room for. Jeff has told you the same thing, that he approved it on my recommendation.

The lawyers I know about for the obvious reason. They structured the deal, and you can't structure a deal without knowing who the principals are. If you're going to tell me that's a failure, I'd say a lot of what gets said on a conference call to approve a financing isn't a recitation of who owns the general partner.

So, the Skilling approval I know firsthand. The rest is how a transaction like that gets done. I've answered it.

The C-Suite.speaker: expert
The C-Suite.message:
I know the document. The foundation put in $25,000, it was a purchase of part of an existing LJM1 limited partner's interest, and it was paid out when the Rhythms position was unwound. Those are the facts, and I'm not going to argue with the arithmetic.

But look at what I told the Board in June 1999. I said the general partner of LJM1 wouldn't receive the appreciated value of the Enron stock. That described my role as GP and the waterfall in the LJM1 structure. Southampton was a separate purchase, in March of 2000, of an interest that a limited partner was selling. The investor on that paper is a family foundation, not me as general partner. You're asking me to read a Board slide from nine months earlier as a promise about every investment anyone connected to me might make later. I don't think that's a fair reading.

The return was large because it was a short-duration investment that worked. Plenty of investors in this market made multiples on short holds.

As for whether anyone should have gone back to the Board or the Office of the Chairman about it, that's a fair question for the people who reviewed these deals. I did my job with the structure in front of me. The Rhythms unwind itself was negotiated and reviewed by Rick Causey's team, and they found it fair.

The C-Suite.message: Is there anything else you think the Committee should know?

The C-Suite.speaker: expert
The C-Suite.message:
Yes. Don't lose sight of what this company is facing. We're in the middle of a confidence crisis, and the market doesn't care about who signed which approval sheet in 1999. It cares whether Enron has liquidity and whether the people running finance can be trusted to keep the banks and the rating agencies with us. I'm the person who does that, and I'd rather be doing it than sitting here relitigating transactions the Board approved.

On the transactions themselves, the structure was built by the Board, not by me. The directors decided what controls to put around LJM. Rick Causey and Rick Buy reviewed the deals, the Audit Committee looked at them every year, and Andersen and Vinson & Elkins signed off. If any of that didn't work as intended, take it up with the people who ran those controls. I'm not going to be the one blamed for a process that other people were responsible for operating.

The restatement is about accounting treatment, and the accounting treatment is Andersen's and Causey's area. I presented deals and the accountants told us how they were booked. Keep that distinction in your report.

I've been straight with you today. If you have more questions, ask them. I'd just ask that you read the whole record, and not only the parts that make a good headline.
